title: binary-kv-serializer-for-multiplexed-websocket-and-worker-queues
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background:
Redwood's current propagation model uses text-based HTTP headers for trace context and a JSON context envelope for richer KV propagation. This works well for REST and gRPC but has two recurring problems: 1) high overhead and fragility over multiplexed transports (WebSocket, SSE) and internal queue messages that prefer compact binary envelopes; 2) inconsistent propagation across async worker pools (sidecar queues, ephemeral fibers) where headers are dropped or re-encoded, causing broken sampling decisions and orphaned spans.

Goal:
Introduce a backward-compatible binary KV serializer and SDK adapters that: 1) provide a compact, signed, and versioned binary header for transporting trace + limited KV context across multiplexed channels and internal queues; 2) ensure sampling decisions and trace identifiers are preserved end-to-end across HTTP, WebSocket, and worker queue boundaries; 3) limit cardinality and avoid leaking PII by enforcing a propagated key whitelist and optional hashing; 4) integrate with existing Redwood trace ingestion without changes to the collector.

Scope and deliverables:
- Binary envelope spec (v1) with wire format, field types, versioning, and HMAC signature for integrity.
- SDK encoders/decoders for Node and Python (Go optional) exposing 2 APIs: attachToTransport(transportType) and reifyToContext().
- Middleware adapters: WebSocket frame encoder/decoder that tucks the binary envelope into a single control frame (no per-message duplication); worker queue adapter that serializes context into message metadata for Redis/NSQ/SQS integrations.
- Sampling propagation semantics: when the binary envelope contains a sampling override it must be honored across async boundaries; SDK will log deterministic sampling transitions as spans.
- Backcompat: SDKs must still accept incoming text headers and the existing JSON envelope. Priority is decode compatibility (binary -> context, JSON -> context). For outgoing over HTTP we default to existing text headers. Binary is used only on transports that advertise support or for internal queue metadata.
- Admin controls in Console: toggle binary propagation per-project, per-route; propagated-keys whitelist (defaults to ["trace_id","sample_rate","route_id"]) and scrubbers with regex-based redact rules.
- Tests: interop matrix across Node server -> Node worker, Python server -> Node worker, WebSocket bridge, and HTTP fallback. Load test to verify envelope adds <1% CPU and <0.5ms p95 end-to-end extra latency for typical messages.

Design notes and trade-offs considered:
- Why a signed binary format? Minimizes size on multiplexed channels and prevents accidental or malicious tampering of sampling overrides. Signed headers add operational complexity (key rotation) but improve safety.
- Why whitelist propagated keys? Prevents high-cardinality telemetry and PII leakage. Trade-off is developer ergonomics; we provide SDK helpers to surface safe keys and to opt-in additional keys per-project.
- Why not modify collector? Keeping collector unchanged reduces rollout risk; SDKs translate binary envelope into existing span attributes before emission. Future collector changes can add native binary handling.

Implementation plan (milestones):
1) Spec draft and security review (2 weeks) - deliver wire format, HMAC scheme, rotation plan.
2) Node SDK encoder/decoder + WebSocket middleware (3 weeks) - internal dogfood for realtime product.
3) Python SDK + queue adapters (2 weeks) - integrate with Celery/RQ/worker-libraries.
4) Console feature flags and propagated-keys UI (2 weeks) - enable/disable controls per project.
5) Interop tests, load tests, and rollout (2 weeks) - staged: internal services -> selected customers -> global.

Rollout and monitoring:
- Phased rollout: internal only -> beta customers (opt-in) -> enabled by default for Dedicated clusters.
- Dashboards to monitor: percent of messages using binary envelope, percent of spans with sampling overrides, rate of signature verification failures, p95 latency delta for affected routes.
- Alerts: signature verification failure rate >0.1% sustained for 10m, propagation loss causing new trace starts downstream >0.5% of requests.

Security considerations:
- HMAC keys stored in KMS; rotation strategy required with grace window.
- Binary parser must be hardened against malformed payloads; fuzz tests mandatory.
- Default propagated-keys whitelist prohibits email/ssn-like keys; any request to add high-cardinality keys triggers a review.

Compatibility matrix:
- HTTP (existing): continue using text headers. Convert binary when internal transport negotiated.
- WebSocket: if client sends SUBSCRIBE-BIN header, use binary control frame for subsequent messages. Fall back to text header otherwise.
- Queues: include envelope in message metadata property "rw_ctx_bin_v1". Consumers with older SDKs will ignore and re-sample; plan to provide shim sidecar for the short term.

Open questions:
- Should binary envelopes include optional TTL for trace propagation across long queues? (security vs observability)
- Key rotation grace semantics: how long to accept signatures from previous keys before rejecting?

Acceptance criteria:
acceptance_criteria: Spec doc merged in RFC repository and security review completed
Node SDK binary encoder/decoder implemented with unit tests and WebSocket middleware integrated in realtime service
Python SDK queue adapters implemented with integration tests for Celery and SQS
Console feature flag and propagated-keys UI merged and available in beta environment
Interoperability tests demonstrate trace continuity across HTTP -> WebSocket -> worker pipeline in 4 cross-language scenarios
Load tests show <1% CPU change and p95 latency delta <0.5ms for representative workloads
Monitoring dashboards emit metrics listed in rollout plan and alert thresholds validated in staging
